findings.title: Chi squared expected counts below five
findings.description: The tool's own output gives expected counts of 2.5 in both infection cells, half the conventional minimum of 5 for the chi-squared approximation; Fisher's exact test is the standard choice at these counts. This is a test-selection issue (rulebook rule 5), not a numerical error, and it does not change the paper's conclusion -- it makes the reported p optimistically precise rather than wrong in direction. Recorded as suspicious rather than higher because uncorrected 2x2 chi-squared on small counts was routine practice in 2009 clinical reporting.

findings.title: Null conclusion without interval or effect size
findings.description: absence_of_evidence could not be run because the paper prints no confidence interval and no coefficient with a standard error, so there is nothing to pass it. The point estimate recoverable from the counts (Fisher odds ratio 1.56, from recalc_chi_squared) actually favours MORE infection in the arm that received fewer antibiotics, and with 3 and 2 events the interval around it would be very wide. This is the ordinary and widespread practice of reading a non-significant p as evidence of no effect; it is a limitation of the inference, not a sign of anything wrong with the numbers.

findings.title: Design powered for a much larger difference
findings.description: This is a reading of the paper's own stated design parameters against its own reported counts, with no calculation. A quantitative sensitivity figure was NOT computed: required_n and verify_power_analysis both need the effect size on the test's own metric (Cohen's h for two proportions), which the paper does not print and which I am not permitted to derive by hand. The paper is commendably explicit about its design assumptions, which is what makes this visible at all; many papers state none.

findings.notes: Both SDs exceed the maximum an age range of 20-29 permits, so the two statements cannot both be literally true. The innocent explanation is strong and is probably the right one: 'in their 20s' reads naturally as loose shorthand for a young-adult cohort rather than a strict inclusion criterion, and the paper states no numeric age range anywhere. A supporting check points the same way -- check_proportion_from_normal on 0 of 28 patients below age 20 gives binomial p = 0.00062 against a normal N(23.9, 5.84) model, but the result explicitly does NOT violate its distribution-free bound [0.0000, 0.6916], so a right-skewed age distribution with a hard floor near 20 explains the SDs and the phrase together. The Discussion also criticises earlier studies for a 'wide range of patient's age', which sits awkwardly beside SDs of nearly 6 years, but that is a rhetorical tension rather than an arithmetic one. Recorded so a reader can see it; not treated as evidence against the paper.

findings.description: A terminology slip: beta = 0.20 is the type II error rate, not the test power. computed.reading: As printed the sentence asserts 20% power alongside alpha = 0.05, which would be an unusable design. The conventional reading is that beta is the type II error rate and power is 1 - beta = 0.80, which is what 28 per group is consistent with.
